contentBlocks.text: Welcome to Civics, Government & Economics. You've learned the three branches of government before — this year, go deeper: why does this structure exist at all?

The US Constitution divides government power across three branches — legislative (Congress, makes laws), executive (the President, enforces laws), judicial (courts, interprets laws) — specifically to prevent any single branch from accumulating too much power. Each branch also has real checks on the others: Congress can override a presidential veto with enough votes, the President nominates judges but the Senate must confirm them, courts can rule a law unconstitutional. This isn't just an org chart — it's a deliberate design choice reflecting a specific concern: that concentrated power, even with good intentions, tends toward abuse over time. Explain, in your own words, why designing a government around 'preventing abuse' is a different goal than designing one purely for 'efficiency.'

Understanding WHY separation of powers exists, not just naming the three branches, is real political-philosophy thinking. Tomorrow we'll look at another structural division: power between national and state government.

objectives: Explain the purpose behind separation of powers, not just name the three branches
Distinguish a government designed to prevent abuse from one designed purely for efficiency
teacherGuide.facilitationScript:
1. Briefly review the three branches as prior knowledge.
2. Introduce the deeper 'why' — preventing concentrated power/abuse, using the veto-override and judicial-nomination examples.
3. Discuss the efficiency-vs-abuse-prevention design tension.
4. Complete the worksheet.
5. Preview tomorrow's topic: federalism.
differentiationTips: Struggling: use a simple analogy — one person holding all the keys to a building (efficient, but risky) vs. requiring two people to agree before opening certain doors (slower, but safer)
Ready for more: ask them to identify a real historical or hypothetical example where one branch's check on another actually mattered
This is the first lesson of the year — a good moment to frame the course as analytical civics, not just structural memorization
teacherGuide.answerKey: 1. Separation of powers exists to prevent any single branch from accumulating too much power. 2. A government designed for efficiency prioritizes speed and simplicity; one designed to prevent abuse deliberately accepts more friction/slowness in exchange for checks on concentrated power.
teacherGuide.standardsRationale: Directly addresses the course's 'how government works' description at a genuinely analytical level appropriate for Grade 12, building on the structural civics content introduced at Grade 8.

generationData.instructions: Answer each question about separation of powers.

prompts.prompt: Why does the Constitution divide power across three branches?
Give one real example of a check one branch has on another.
Why is 'preventing abuse' a different design goal than 'efficiency'?
